x: Melting ice only changes state from solid to liquid and no new substance forms, so it is physical. Rusting, curdling and burning all make new substances.
t: Check each change for a new substance.

x: Option B is incorrect: physical changes usually involve little energy change, while chemical changes often release or absorb a lot of heat or light. Mass is conserved in both.
t: Discriminate the features of physical and chemical changes.

x: Both are true and R explains A: photosynthesis turns CO₂ and water into new substances, glucose and oxygen, which makes it chemical.
t: Check whether R shows a new substance forming.

x: Both are true: dissolved salt can be recovered by evaporation, so dissolving is physical, while electrolysis makes new gases, hydrogen and oxygen, so it is chemical.
t: Check whether the original substance can be recovered.

x: All three are correct: melting and freezing reverse each other, burning paper is chemical and cannot be undone, and broken glass stays glass, so the change is physical even though it cannot be reversed.
t: Discriminate reversible/irreversible from physical/chemical.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Melting and freezing are reversible physical changes.
II. Burning of paper is an irreversible chemical change.
III. Breaking or cutting glass is an irreversible physical change.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

x: Rusting is prevented by painting and galvanising, burning fuels powers cooking and transport, photosynthesis makes food and oxygen, and electrolysis gives hydrogen and oxygen, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the use or remedy linked with each change.

x: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, formed when iron meets oxygen and moisture.
t: Recall the formula of rust.

x: Two are physical: melting ice and magnetising iron, since neither forms a new substance. Rusting and curd formation are chemical.
t: Check each change for a new substance.

x: Both are true and R explains A: an acid and a base react to give salt and water, so antacids neutralise stomach acid and lime treats acidic soil.
t: Check whether R is the reaction behind A.

x: Boiling turns liquid into gas throughout the liquid at the boiling point, evaporation happens only at the surface at any temperature, freezing turns liquid into solid and condensation turns steam into water, giving a-i, b-iii, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Separate boiling from evaporation by where and at what temperature each occurs.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Boiling of water
(b) Evaporation of water
(c) Freezing of water
(d) Condensation of steam

List-II
(i) Liquid turns to gas throughout its bulk at a fixed temperature
(ii) Liquid changes into a solid
(iii) Liquid turns to vapour only at its surface, at any temperature
(iv) Steam changes into water

x: Both are true: salt and sugar both dissolve evenly in water to form true solutions.
t: Recall examples of true solutions.

x: All four are correct: breaking chalk, stretching rubber and cutting paper or wood change only size or shape, so they are physical changes.
t: Check each change for a new substance.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: unchanged composition is a general feature of physical change, while expansion happens because heated particles move further apart.
t: Check whether R is a cause or a general fact.

x: Both are true: camphor and ammonium chloride sublime, going straight from solid to vapour without changing identity.
t: Recall common subliming substances.

x: All four are correct: burning wood gives ash, CO₂ and water, burning candle wax gives CO₂ and water vapour, cooking makes new compounds and digestion breaks down large molecules, so all are chemical changes.
t: Recall examples of chemical change.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Burning wood forms ash, carbon dioxide, and water.
II. Burning a candle forms carbon dioxide and water vapour.
III. Cooking and baking food form new compounds.
IV. Digestion of food breaks down complex molecules.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

x: Both are true: a physical change keeps composition the same, and evaporation and condensation reverse each other.
t: Recall the features of physical change.

x: Curd forms when lactic acid bacteria (Lactobacillus) ferment lactose into lactic acid, which sets the milk protein. The other options describe digestion, respiration and neutralisation.
t: Recall the microbe and sugar in curd formation.

x: Camphor and NH₄Cl show sublimation and deposition, salt in water shows dissolution and crystallisation, and metals show expansion and contraction, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
t: Recall examples of reversible physical changes.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the double arrow in N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ shows that the reaction runs both ways and reaches equilibrium.
t: Check whether R shows the reversibility in A.

x: I, II and IV are correct: burning, cooking, digestion and explosions are chemical changes. III is false because souring of milk is an irreversible chemical change.
t: Discriminate souring from simple physical changes.

x: Both are true: ice melts when heat overcomes the forces between water molecules, and melting matters in cooling, refrigeration and weather.
t: Recall the cause and uses of melting.

x: Neutralisation is used in industrial processes as well as antacids and soil treatment. IV saline uses dissolving salt and electrolysis gives hydrogen and oxygen.
t: Recall the uses of neutralisation.

x: Both are true: Lactobacillus turns milk into curd, and curd helps preserve food and adds nutrition.
t: Recall the microbe in curd formation.

x: Both are true: dissolving salt only spreads out its ions, and salt solution is used in cooking and intravenous saline.
t: Recall dissolving as a physical change.

x: Both are true and R explains A: souring forms lactic acid, a new substance, which makes it a chemical change.
t: Check whether R shows a new substance forming.

x: Fireworks explode by fast combustion that forms new gases and compounds with heat, light and sound. Water decomposition, lactic acid and rust belong to other changes.
t: Recall explosion as a chemical change.

x: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent with the same composition throughout. Colloids scatter light and suspensions are heterogeneous.
t: Discriminate solutions from colloids and suspensions.

x: Option A is incorrect: a true solution's particles are too small to be filtered out. It is stable, invisible to the eye and shows no Tyndall effect.
t: Recall the properties of a true solution.

x: Both are true and R explains A: when solute–solvent forces equal the original forces, mixing absorbs or releases no heat, so ΔH_mix = 0.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Smoke is a solid aerosol, milk an emulsion, jelly a gel and whipped cream a foam, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Recall one example of each colloid type.

x: I and II are correct: a solid aerosol is solid in gas and an emulsion is liquid in liquid. III is false because a gel has a liquid dispersed phase in a solid dispersion medium, as in jelly or cheese.
t: Recall which phase is dispersed and which is the medium for each colloid type.

x: Both are true: solubility is defined at a stated temperature and pressure, and "like dissolves like" means polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents.
t: Recall the factors affecting solubility.

x: Reverse osmosis pushes water through a membrane against the osmotic gradient, leaving salts and bacteria behind, so it desalinates and purifies water.
t: Discriminate osmosis from reverse osmosis.

x: Both are true: the solute is what dissolves, and the solvent, usually present in larger amount, does the dissolving.
t: Discriminate solute from solvent.

x: All three are correct: in a gaseous solution both solute and solvent are gases, as in air, where oxygen is dissolved in nitrogen.
t: Recall examples of each solution type.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. A gaseous solution has a gas as its solute.
II. A gaseous solution has a gas as its solvent.
III. Air is a gaseous solution of oxygen in nitrogen.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

x: Oxygen in water is gas in liquid, ethanol in water liquid in liquid, and salt in water solid in liquid, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii.
t: Recall examples of each solution type.

x: Option C is incorrect: sucrose is a solid, so sugar in water is a solid-in-liquid solution. The other statements about solid-in-liquid solutions are right.
t: Check the state of each solute.

x: Both are true and R explains A: hydrogen is the gaseous solute and palladium the solid solvent, which defines a gas-in-solid solution.
t: Check whether R gives the definition behind A.

x: Both are true: in a liquid-in-solid solution the solute is liquid and the solvent solid, as in a mercury–gold amalgam.
t: Recall amalgam as a liquid-in-solid solution.

x: Both features apply: a solid-in-solid solution, such as an alloy like brass, has a solid solute dissolved in a solid solvent.
t: Name both components of the solution type before choosing.
s:
Which of the following characteristics apply to a solid-in-solid solution?
1. It has a solid as its solute.
2. It has a solid as its solvent.

x: I, II and III are correct: alloys are solid solutions, brass is copper with zinc and bronze is copper with tin. IV is false because it gives bronze's makeup for brass.
t: Discriminate brass (Cu + Zn) from bronze (Cu + Sn).
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Alloys are examples of solid-in-solid solutions.
II. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
III. Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.
IV. Brass is an alloy of copper and tin.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

x: Both are true: an unsaturated solution can take more solute, while a saturated one holds the most possible at that temperature and pressure, leaving the rest undissolved.
t: Discriminate unsaturated from saturated solutions.

x: All five are ways to express solubility or concentration: g per 100 g solvent, g per 100 mL, molarity, molality and mole fraction.
t: Recall the units of concentration.

x: All four are correct: dust is a solid aerosol, and a liquid aerosol has liquid droplets in gas, as in cloud, mist and fog.
t: Recall the dispersed phase and medium of aerosols.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Dust is a solid aerosol.
II. A liquid aerosol has a liquid dispersed phase.
III. A liquid aerosol has a gas dispersion medium.
IV. Cloud, mist and fog are liquid aerosols.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

x: Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil in water, cheese is a gel, soap lather is a foam of gas in liquid and dust is a solid aerosol, giving a-i, b-iii, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Identify the dispersed phase and medium of each everyday colloid.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Mayonnaise
(b) Cheese
(c) Soap lather
(d) Dust

List-II
(i) Emulsion
(ii) Foam
(iii) Gel
(iv) Solid aerosol

x: Both are true and R explains A: a sol is defined as a solid dispersed in a liquid.
t: Check whether R restates A.

x: All four are correct: gold and sulphur sols are sols, and a solid sol has solid in solid, as in coloured glass, gems and ruby glass.
t: Discriminate sol (solid in liquid) from solid sol (solid in solid).

x: All four are correct: foam is gas in liquid, solid foam is gas in solid, and pumice and foam rubber are solid foams.
t: Discriminate foam from solid foam.

x: Both are true and R explains A: ruby glass owes its colour to tiny gold particles dispersed in glass, a solid in solid, which is a solid sol and hence a colloid.
t: Name the dispersed phase and medium to see whether R accounts for A.
s:
Assertion (A): Ruby glass is a colloid.
Reason (R): In ruby glass, fine gold particles are dispersed in solid glass, making it a solid sol.

x: All four are correct: soap lather is a foam of gas in liquid, and solid foams such as pumice and foam rubber are gas in solid.
t: Discriminate foam from solid foam.

x: Osmosis is the movement of solvent, not solute, through a semipermeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution.
t: Recall that only the solvent moves in osmosis.

x: In osmosis water is the solvent, it moves from low to high solute concentration, roots absorb water this way, and reverse osmosis applies pressure on the concentrated side, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the direction of solvent flow in osmosis and RO.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Solvent involved in osmosis
(b) Direction of solvent movement in osmosis
(c) Process by which plant roots absorb water
(d) Side on which external pressure is applied in reverse osmosis

List-II
(i) Concentrated side
(ii) Water
(iii) Low solute concentration to high solute concentration
(iv) Osmosis

x: Both are true: a concentrated solution has much solute relative to solvent, and a dilute solution has little.
t: Discriminate concentrated from dilute solutions.
